obligations: A developer shall make available to each deployer of its covered ADMT a general statement of intended and known harmful uses, categories of training data, known limitations, instructions for appropriate use and meaningful human review, and information reasonably necessary for deployer compliance, in a form that protects trade secrets (Sec. 6-1-1702(1))

A developer shall provide each deployer notice of material updates, intentional and substantial modifications, and changes to intended use, limitations, or risk mitigation within a reasonable time, and may use public release notes with direct notice (Sec. 6-1-1702(2))
A developer shall retain records reasonably necessary to demonstrate compliance for at least three years, including version identifiers, changelogs, and notices of material updates (Sec. 6-1-1702(4))

A deployer shall retain records reasonably necessary to demonstrate compliance for at least three years after a consequential decision, including version identifiers, changelogs, and documentation of material mitigation changes (Sec. 6-1-1703)

Prior to using a covered ADMT to materially influence a consequential decision, a deployer shall provide a clear and conspicuous notice to the consumer that it used or will use a covered ADMT and instructions for obtaining additional information (Sec. 6-1-1704(1))
A deployer may comply with the prior notice by maintaining a prominent public notice reasonably accessible at points of consumer interaction (Sec. 6-1-1704(2))

If a covered ADMT materially influences a consequential decision resulting in an adverse outcome, the deployer shall provide within thirty days a plain language description of the decision and the ADMT's role, instructions and process to request additional information including ADMT name, version, developer, and types of personal data used, and an explanation of consumer rights under section 6-1-1705 (Sec. 6-1-1704(3))
A deployer or developer shall provide notices and disclosures in a manner reasonably accessible to consumers with disabilities and limited English proficiency (Sec. 6-1-1704(8))

When a consumer experiences an adverse outcome from a consequential decision materially influenced by a covered ADMT, the deployer shall provide instructions for requesting and correcting factually incorrect or materially inaccurate personal data and an opportunity for meaningful human review and reconsideration to the extent commercially reasonable (Sec. 6-1-1705(1)(a))
The attorney general shall adopt rules to clarify post adverse outcome disclosures by January 1, 2027 (Sec. 6-1-1704(4)(b))
The attorney general shall adopt rules to clarify and implement consumer rights by January 1, 2027 (Sec. 6-1-1705(3))
A deployer subject to FERPA satisfies notice and disclosure requirements through FERPA consistent processes and is not required to establish separate processes (Sec. 6-1-1704(9))
prohibitions: A contract provision that purports to indemnify, defend, or hold harmless a developer or deployer from liability for damages resulting from its own acts or omissions related to use of ADMT in consequential decisions in violation of the Colorado Anti Discrimination Act or other Colorado anti discrimination law is contrary to public policy and void (Sec. 6-1-1707(7)(a))

What it does

This part regulates automated decision-making technology used to materially influence consequential decisions in Colorado. It imposes documentation and update duties on developers, record keeping and disclosure duties on deployers, and correction and human review rights for consumers. The attorney general enforces it as a deceptive trade practice, with no new private right of action.

Who it applies to

  • Developers doing business in Colorado that develop, offer, sell, lease, license, or otherwise make commercially available a covered ADMT (Sec. 6-1-1701(8))
  • Deployers doing business in Colorado that deploy a covered ADMT (Sec. 6-1-1701(7))
  • Consumers, including employees, job applicants who are Colorado residents, and individuals whose access to, eligibility for, or opportunity in Colorado is evaluated in a consequential decision by a person doing business in Colorado (Sec. 6-1-1701(4))

Effective date

January 1, 2027, except sections 6-1-1704(4), 6-1-1705(3), 6-1-1706(6), 10-3-1104.9(3)(e), section 4, section 5, and section 6 take effect upon passage; applies to consequential decisions made on or after January 1, 2027 (Sec. 5)

Key definitions

  • Adverse outcome: a decision that denies, terminates, revokes, or materially reduces or restricts access to or provision of an opportunity or service, or results in materially less favorable differentiated price or terms compared to similarly situated consumers (Sec. 6-1-1701(1))
  • Automated decision-making technology or ADMT: technology that processes personal data and uses computation to generate output used to make, guide, or assist a decision about an individual, excluding listed technologies and certain tools (Sec. 6-1-1701(2))
  • Consequential decision: a decision about a consumer relating to a covered domain or differentiated terms that materially limit access to a covered domain, excluding low-stakes, advertising, and other listed activities (Sec. 6-1-1701(3))
  • Covered ADMT: automated decision-making technology used to materially influence a consequential decision (Sec. 6-1-1701(5))
  • Covered domain: education enrollment or opportunity, employment or employment opportunity, lease or purchase of residential real estate in Colorado, financial or lending service, insurance, health care services, or essential government services and public benefits (Sec. 6-1-1701(6))
  • Deployer: a person doing business in Colorado that deploys a covered ADMT (Sec. 6-1-1701(7))
  • Developer: a person doing business in Colorado that develops, offers, sells, leases, licenses, or otherwise makes commercially available a covered ADMT, develops a component designed for use as part of a covered ADMT, or intentionally and substantially modifies an ADMT into a covered ADMT, with exclusions (Sec. 6-1-1701(8))
  • Materially influence: an ADMT output is a non de minimis factor used in making a consequential decision and affects the outcome, excluding incidental, trivial, or clerical uses (Sec. 6-1-1701(13))
  • Meaningful human review: review by an individual designated by the deployer with authority to approve, modify, or override a consequential decision who considers relevant primary evidence, is trained, does not default to system output, and has access to sufficient information about intended use, limitations, inputs, and principal factors (Sec. 6-1-1701(15))
  • Material update: an update, patch, release, revision, or new version likely to materially affect outputs or performance relevant to intended use or stated intended use, excluding routine maintenance, cosmetic changes, or bug fixes (Sec. 6-1-1701(14))
  • Consumer: has the meaning in section 6-1-1303(6)(a) and includes an employee, a job applicant who is a Colorado resident, and any individual whose access to, eligibility for, or opportunity in Colorado is evaluated in a consequential decision by a person doing business in Colorado (Sec. 6-1-1701(4))
  • Personal data: has the meaning set forth in section 6-1-1303(17) (Sec. 6-1-1701(16))
  • Trade secret: has the meaning set forth in section 7-74-102(4) (Sec. 6-1-1701(17))

Obligations

  • A developer shall make available to each deployer of its covered ADMT a general statement of intended and known harmful uses, categories of training data, known limitations, instructions for appropriate use and meaningful human review, and information reasonably necessary for deployer compliance, in a form that protects trade secrets (Sec. 6-1-1702(1))
  • A developer shall provide each deployer notice of material updates, intentional and substantial modifications, and changes to intended use, limitations, or risk mitigation within a reasonable time, and may use public release notes with direct notice (Sec. 6-1-1702(2))
  • A developer shall retain records reasonably necessary to demonstrate compliance for at least three years, including version identifiers, changelogs, and notices of material updates (Sec. 6-1-1702(4))
  • A deployer shall retain records reasonably necessary to demonstrate compliance for at least three years after a consequential decision, including version identifiers, changelogs, and documentation of material mitigation changes (Sec. 6-1-1703)
  • Prior to using a covered ADMT to materially influence a consequential decision, a deployer shall provide a clear and conspicuous notice to the consumer that it used or will use a covered ADMT and instructions for obtaining additional information (Sec. 6-1-1704(1))
  • A deployer may comply with the prior notice by maintaining a prominent public notice reasonably accessible at points of consumer interaction (Sec. 6-1-1704(2))
  • If a covered ADMT materially influences a consequential decision resulting in an adverse outcome, the deployer shall provide within thirty days a plain language description of the decision and the ADMT's role, instructions and process to request additional information including ADMT name, version, developer, and types of personal data used, and an explanation of consumer rights under section 6-1-1705 (Sec. 6-1-1704(3))
  • A deployer or developer shall provide notices and disclosures in a manner reasonably accessible to consumers with disabilities and limited English proficiency (Sec. 6-1-1704(8))
  • When a consumer experiences an adverse outcome from a consequential decision materially influenced by a covered ADMT, the deployer shall provide instructions for requesting and correcting factually incorrect or materially inaccurate personal data and an opportunity for meaningful human review and reconsideration to the extent commercially reasonable (Sec. 6-1-1705(1)(a))
  • The attorney general shall adopt rules to clarify post adverse outcome disclosures by January 1, 2027 (Sec. 6-1-1704(4)(b))
  • The attorney general shall adopt rules to clarify and implement consumer rights by January 1, 2027 (Sec. 6-1-1705(3))
  • A deployer subject to FERPA satisfies notice and disclosure requirements through FERPA consistent processes and is not required to establish separate processes (Sec. 6-1-1704(9))

Prohibitions

  • A contract provision that purports to indemnify, defend, or hold harmless a developer or deployer from liability for damages resulting from its own acts or omissions related to use of ADMT in consequential decisions in violation of the Colorado Anti Discrimination Act or other Colorado anti discrimination law is contrary to public policy and void (Sec. 6-1-1707(7)(a))

Penalties and enforcement

The attorney general enforces this part through the Colorado Consumer Protection Act; violations of sections 6-1-1702, 6-1-1703, 6-1-1704, and 6-1-1705 are enforceable exclusively by the attorney general (Sec. 6-1-1706(1)). A violation is a deceptive trade practice subject to the Colorado Consumer Protection Act (Sec. 6-1-1706(2)(a); Sec. 6-1-105(1)(uuuu)). Before enforcement, the attorney general shall issue a notice of violation and allow a 60 day cure period if cure is possible, unless the violation is knowing or repeated; a court may consider cure as a mitigating factor (Sec. 6-1-1706(3)(a)-(d)). The cure period subsection is repealed effective January 1, 2030 (Sec. 6-1-1706(3)(f)). No new private right of action is created, and existing rights and remedies are not limited (Sec. 6-1-1706(4); Sec. 6-1-1709(1)). Specific penalty amounts are not stated in the text.

How it affects AI deployment

  • An organisation deploying a covered ADMT must determine whether its technology is a covered ADMT used to materially influence a consequential decision in a covered domain (Sec. 6-1-1701(3),(5),(6),(13))
  • It must obtain from the developer the documentation required by section 6-1-1702(1) and receive notices of material updates (Sec. 6-1-1702(1),(2))
  • It must provide a clear and conspicuous pre use notice or maintain a prominent public notice at points of consumer interaction (Sec. 6-1-1704(1),(2))
  • If an adverse outcome occurs, it must provide post adverse outcome disclosures within thirty days, including a plain language description, information about the ADMT and personal data, and consumer rights (Sec. 6-1-1704(3))
  • It must retain records for at least three years to demonstrate compliance (Sec. 6-1-1703)
  • It must provide consumers with correction rights for factually incorrect or materially inaccurate personal data and an opportunity for meaningful human review and reconsideration (Sec. 6-1-1705(1))
  • It must ensure notices and disclosures are accessible to consumers with disabilities and limited English proficiency (Sec. 6-1-1704(8))
  • If it is subject to FERPA, it may use existing FERPA notice, correction, and review processes instead of separate processes (Sec. 6-1-1704(9); Sec. 6-1-1705(2))
  • If it is an insurer subject to section 10-3-1104.9, it is deemed compliant in the practice of insurance, except for employment uses (Sec. 6-1-1708(1),(2))
  • If it is a HIPAA covered entity or business associate, most sections do not apply except for employment decisions, and it must provide a general notice of advanced technologies and specific disclosures for financial assistance eligibility (Sec. 6-1-1708(3))
  • It should monitor attorney general rules clarifying materially influence, post adverse outcome disclosures, and consumer rights (Sec. 6-1-1704(4); Sec. 6-1-1705(3); Sec. 6-1-1706(5))

Notable exemptions

  • Technologies excluded from ADMT: anti malware, anti virus, calculators, databases, data storage, firewalls, internet domain registration, internet website loading, networking, spam and robocall filtering, spell checking, spreadsheets requiring human analysis without machine learning, web caching, web hosting, tools used solely to summarize or present information for human review, and certain natural language communication tools not intended for consequential decisions (Sec. 6-1-1701(2)(b))
  • Consequential decision exclusions: low stakes or routine decisions, advertising, marketing, differentiated product recommendations, search, content moderation, spreadsheets requiring manual human analysis, actions where ADMT only summarizes or presents information without producing a score or inference, narrow procedural tasks, cybersecurity and fraud prevention activities, economic sanctions compliance, and routine academic administration (Sec. 6-1-1701(3)(b))
  • Developer exclusions: persons developing and using ADMT solely for research or internal purposes without making it available to another person, preceding developers whose ADMT is modified by an unaffiliated person, and persons whose component is integrated into a covered ADMT without actual knowledge (Sec. 6-1-1701(8)(b))
  • Insurers and affiliated entities subject to section 10-3-1104.9 are in compliance with this part in the practice of insurance, except for employment uses (Sec. 6-1-1708(1),(2))
  • HIPAA covered entities and business associates are exempt from sections 6-1-1701 through 6-1-1706 except for employment decisions, with specific notice requirements for financial assistance eligibility (Sec. 6-1-1708(3))
  • Medical devices subject to FDA oversight and pharmaceutical or medical device manufacturer research and development subject to FDA oversight are exempt from sections 6-1-1701 through 6-1-1706 (Sec. 6-1-1708(4))
  • A creditor that provides a notice under ECOA and FCRA that also satisfies this section's notice requirements is not required to provide a separate notice (Sec. 6-1-1704(6))
  • A deployer is not required to disclose trade secrets or information protected from disclosure by state or federal law, but must notify the consumer if it withholds information (Sec. 6-1-1704(5))
  • A person is not required to make disclosures that would be prohibited by federal law or compromise cybersecurity, fraud prevention, anti money laundering, counter terrorist financing, or economic sanctions compliance programs (Sec. 6-1-1704(7))
  • A deployer subject to FERPA is not required to establish separate notice, disclosure, correction, or human review processes if it has FERPA compliant processes (Sec. 6-1-1704(9); Sec. 6-1-1705(2))
  • This part does not require disclosure of nonpublic personal information in violation of the Gramm Leach Bliley Act (Sec. 6-1-1708(6))

Compliance steps

  • Classify whether the technology is a covered ADMT and whether the decision is a consequential decision in a covered domain, using definitions and exclusions (Sec. 6-1-1701(2),(3),(5),(6),(13))
  • If acting as a developer, prepare and provide the required documentation to deployers, including intended uses, training data categories, limitations, and instructions (Sec. 6-1-1702(1))
  • If acting as a developer, establish a process to notify deployers of material updates and retain records for at least three years (Sec. 6-1-1702(2),(4))
  • If acting as a deployer, obtain and review developer documentation and update notices (Sec. 6-1-1702(1),(2))
  • Implement a pre use consumer notice or a prominent public notice at points of consumer interaction (Sec. 6-1-1704(1),(2))
  • Create a process to provide post adverse outcome disclosures within thirty days, including plain language description, ADMT information, and consumer rights (Sec. 6-1-1704(3))
  • Establish a process for consumers to request correction of factually incorrect or materially inaccurate personal data and meaningful human review and reconsideration (Sec. 6-1-1705(1))
  • Retain records for at least three years to demonstrate compliance (Sec. 6-1-1703)
  • Ensure notices and disclosures are accessible to consumers with disabilities and limited English proficiency (Sec. 6-1-1704(8))
  • If subject to FERPA, HIPAA, insurance, or other sector specific laws, integrate compliance with existing processes and exemptions (Sec. 6-1-1704(9); Sec. 6-1-1705(2); Sec. 6-1-1708)
  • Monitor and implement attorney general rules on post adverse outcome disclosures, consumer rights, and materially influence (Sec. 6-1-1704(4); Sec. 6-1-1705(3); Sec. 6-1-1706(5))
